title: A reliable real-time monitor of conscious experience during anesthesia

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a noninvasive monitor that continuously estimates whether an anesthetized patient is aware of the surrounding world, having an internal experience disconnected from it, or showing no reportable experience. Connected awareness includes experiencing the operating room; disconnected experience could include dreamlike experience without awareness of the surroundings. The intended advance is to distinguish these experiential states reliably enough to inform care, including situations in which a patient cannot move or subsequently remember what happened. These distinctions define the target capability; the supplied evidence does not demonstrate that a monitor already achieves them.

Existing EEG monitors provide a foundation, but their numerical indices do not consistently map to a single clinical state across anesthetic drugs and devices. A monitor of conscious experience would therefore need a stronger connection between its measurements and the patient's experiential state than an improved numerical index alone. Absence of a report would also need careful interpretation: it can leave experience uncertain rather than establish that experience was absent.

significance.text: If credibly validated, the monitor would make clinically important information available while an operation is happening: whether the patient may be experiencing the surroundings despite absent movement or later recall. The practical motivation is illustrated by the reviewed EEG study, in which some patients responded to verbal commands during emergence while monitor indices remained below 60. A reliable experiential-state measurement could help clinicians recognize unwanted awareness sooner and support timely intervention. Preventing harm would additionally require effective responses to the readings and evidence that those responses improve outcomes.

Conditional significance: distinguishing connected awareness from disconnected experience could also provide a research instrument for studying how anesthetic drugs alter consciousness. The revolutionary step would be dependable measurement of experience, beyond the measurement of responsiveness or an EEG pattern. Such a device would not automatically explain why consciousness changes, prove the absence of all subjective experience, or establish safe anesthetic dosing by itself. Extension to brain injury or other neurological conditions would require separate validation.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved target is a validated mapping from noninvasive physiological measurements to the three proposed experiential categories, with sufficient temporal precision to guide decisions during anesthesia. The supplied study establishes a narrower obstacle: processed EEG indices can behave differently across drugs and devices, and a particular index value need not correspond to the same clinical state. It does not establish the complete absence of the broader proposed capability across contemporary research, all age groups or neurological conditions.

Validation challenge, synthesized from the proposed goal: experience is difficult to label when the patient cannot communicate. Movement, a response to a command, later recall, drug concentration and processed EEG readings address different aspects of the situation; treating any one of them as a complete reference would require justification. Carefully timed reports can describe accessible experience, while postoperative interviews concern remembered experience. Missing reports leave a particular uncertainty about experiences that were neither communicated nor retained. The supplied evidence does not establish the performance of every reference or justify an absolute claim that every possible unreported experience is experimentally unverifiable.

Engineering requirements inferred from these limitations include identifying signals that retain their meaning across anesthetic regimens, distinguishing physiological transitions from measurement artifacts, and producing timely estimates with calibrated uncertainty. Generalization would have to be demonstrated across relevant ages and neurological conditions rather than assumed from a narrow sample. The reviewed emergence study motivates this concern but does not itself resolve it: its homogeneous population, retrospective analysis and replayed EEG constrain how far its findings can be transferred to real-time monitoring throughout surgery.

current_state.text: Processed EEG monitors already exist. Marlene Lipp and colleagues' study, published online on 18 December 2023, enrolled 45 adults receiving three anesthetic regimens and analyzed 43 after two exclusions. Its retrospective analysis used replayed EEG to examine monitoring during emergence. Index behavior depended on both the anesthetic regimen and the device, supporting interpretation alongside the administered drugs and raw EEG rather than reliance on an index value in isolation.

The study included testing responses to verbal commands during induction and emergence using the isolated forearm technique. Some patients, particularly in the BIS and total intravenous anesthesia group, responded during emergence despite indices below 60. This documents a mismatch between index interpretation and responsiveness; it does not demonstrate detection of disconnected experience or unremembered awareness. The homogeneous sample, emergence setting and replay methodology limit generalization to other populations and continuous intraoperative use. The supplied review assessed the full extracted article text but did not inspect its figure images; its qualitative conclusions relied on textual methods and results.

The research summary also describes a purported randomized trial by Shiv Lal Soni and colleagues, reportedly published online on 10 September 2026, involving 674 elective-surgery patients and comparing BIS-guided care with end-tidal anesthetic gas guidance. It reports no statistically significant difference in recalled awareness. These details remain unverified in the supplied evidence review: although the research summary says an indexed abstract was available, the retained PubMed material available to the reviewer contained only a cookie-access barrier, without identifying article content or results. The full paper was not inspected. Consequently, the sample size, design, publication details and outcome cannot be treated here as established findings. This access limitation does not show that the reported trial or result is false.

Interpretive limitation: even if the reported nonsignificant trial result is confirmed, lack of a statistically significant difference would not by itself establish equivalence between the two guidance strategies. An endpoint based on recalled awareness would also leave experiences without later recall outside its direct measurement. More broadly, the supplied material supports specific limitations of existing EEG monitoring, but does not establish the entire contemporary capability landscape or prove that no system achieves any part of the proposed three-state distinction.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: prospectively registered studies should specify the experiential categories, the clinical decisions the monitor is intended to support, and how the timing of readings will be aligned with reference observations. Validation should combine carefully timed reports, isolated forearm responses where appropriate and structured postoperative interviews. Each reference should retain its own interpretation, so disagreement is examined rather than hidden inside a single label. The reviewed study demonstrates the relevance of isolated forearm testing, but does not validate this entire proposed protocol or establish a complete reference for subjective experience.
completion_criteria.label: Preregistered validation aligns monitor readings with distinct experiential references

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence of reliability: independent teams should reproduce performance across specified anesthetic regimens and relevant patient populations, including the transitions and operating conditions in which the device would be used. Evaluation should report errors for each experiential category, uncertainty calibration, detection delays and circumstances in which the monitor cannot provide a dependable estimate. Acceptance thresholds should be justified for the intended clinical use and declared before testing; the supplied evidence establishes no numerical standard. Finite studies would establish demonstrated breadth within tested conditions, not literal universality across all drugs, patients or experiences.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce experiential-state performance across specified anesthesia conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence of clinical utility: a prospective comparison should test whether clinicians acting on the monitor's readings improve patient outcomes, including prevention of unwanted awareness and avoidance of harms from unnecessary intervention. Measurement accuracy and useful clinical action are separate requirements. For states lacking an adequate reference, performance should remain explicitly uncertain, with that limitation visible in the device's claims and interpretation. Applications to brain injury or other settings should undergo their own validation rather than inherit approval from anesthesia studies.
completion_criteria.label: Monitor-guided clinical decisions improve patient outcomes in prospective comparison

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ANS-01, A causal theory of anesthetic-induced unconsciousness, concerns why anesthetics change consciousness; ANS-02 concerns measuring the patient's state in real time. A causal theory could guide signal selection and interpretation, while a validated monitor could supply observations that test theories. Neither achievement automatically establishes the other.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-04, Surgical unconsciousness with preserved breathing and circulatory control, concerns producing a desired anesthetic state while preserving physiological function. ANS-06, Broad, active reversal of general anesthesia, concerns actively ending anesthetic effects. ANS-02 could help assess unconsciousness and recovery during either intervention, but monitoring does not itself produce unconsciousness, preserve cardiorespiratory control or reverse anesthesia.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-03, A broadly applicable, pain-selective surgical nerve block, and ANS-07, Systemic, non-opioid analgesia for severe perioperative pain, concern pain control through different interventions. ANS-09, Mechanism-based prevention of chronic postsurgical pain, concerns preventing a longer-term pain outcome. Conscious experience and pain control are distinct targets: a monitor of awareness would not by itself establish adequate analgesia or prevention of chronic pain. These entries retain separate intervention and validation requirements.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-05, A radically accessible, resilient anesthesia platform for essential surgery, could incorporate reliable monitoring, but adds requirements concerning access, resilience and delivery of anesthesia. ANS-08, Reliable rescue oxygenation in the difficult airway, addresses an airway emergency that consciousness monitoring cannot resolve. ANS-10, Mechanism-guided anesthesia to prevent postoperative brain dysfunction, could use measurements of intraoperative state, but predicting or preventing postoperative brain dysfunction would require additional mechanistic and outcome evidence.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish whether any contemporary system achieves the full three-state distinction, or how much of that capability has been demonstrated across drugs, ages and neurological conditions. The review reports an empty bounded search record, so research freshness remains unassessed.

The purported 2026 trial's identity, publication date, sample size, randomized design and recalled-awareness results require accessible identifying content and results. The research summary's abstract account cannot be reconciled with the retained cookie-barrier material from the supplied inputs.
An adequate reference for disconnected or unreported experience remains unresolved. Complementary measures can improve validation without guaranteeing that every subjective experience is captured.
Clinically acceptable error rates, detection delays, uncertainty thresholds and responses to monitor alerts remain to be specified and justified for particular uses.
Whether acting on the proposed monitor improves outcomes, and whether its measurements transfer to brain injury or other neurological conditions, remains undemonstrated in the supplied evidence.

brief.title: Knowing what patients experience under anesthesia
possible: During surgery, clinicians could continuously estimate whether a patient is aware of the operating room, having a dreamlike experience disconnected from it, or showing no reportable experience. A noninvasive monitor could distinguish these states even when the patient cannot move or later remember.
why: Clinicians could recognize unwanted awareness sooner and intervene while surgery is happening. Distinguishing awareness of the surroundings from internal experience would also help researchers study how anesthetic drugs change consciousness.

sources.who: Marlene Lipp and colleagues, Technical University of Munich
sources.showed: They replayed recordings of brain electrical activity through anesthesia monitors. The resulting scores varied with the drugs and devices used during recovery.
sources.quote: Systematic differences of EEG-based indices depend on the drugs and devices used.
sources.cited_for: A monitor score can mean different things depending on the anesthetic drug and device.
sources.not_established: The study did not distinguish dreamlike experience, awareness without later recall, and no reportable experience.

sources.showed: A randomized trial compared care guided by a brainwave score (BIS) with exhaled anesthetic gas targets (MAC). It found no statistically significant difference in recalled awareness.
sources.quote: This randomised trial found that neither BIS nor minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) demonstrated superiority in terms of intraoperative awareness.
sources.cited_for: The trial compared existing guidance methods using remembered awareness as an outcome.
sources.not_established: A nonsignificant difference does not establish equivalence, and interviews cannot directly measure experiences patients do not remember.

shown: Existing monitors turn brain electrical activity into numerical scores. In Lipp and colleagues’ small study, some patients followed commands while recovering despite scores within the recommended surgical range. The analysis used replayed recordings from 43 adults.
Soni and colleagues tested whether existing monitoring methods reduced remembered awareness. Neither study demonstrated continuous recognition of the proposed experiential states throughout surgery.
missing: Measurements still need a validated link to awareness of the surroundings, disconnected internal experience, and no reportable experience.
A dependable way to assess experience when patients cannot communicate or later remember remains unresolved.
Reliable, timely readings need demonstration across anesthetic drugs, patient groups and changing conditions during surgery.
Clinical comparisons need to show that acting on readings prevents unwanted awareness without causing harm through unnecessary intervention.

milestones.label: Readings align with distinct measures of experience
milestones.explanation: Studies registered before testing would have to align readings with timed reports, hand responses to commands where appropriate, and postoperative interviews. This would test the link to experience while preserving disagreements.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce performance across anesthesia conditions
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce performance across specified drugs, patient groups and transitions, measuring errors, delays and uncertainty against predeclared standards. This would establish where readings are dependable.

milestones.label: Monitor-guided care improves patient outcomes
milestones.explanation: A prospective comparison would have to show that acting on readings improves outcomes, including unwanted awareness and harms from unnecessary intervention. This would establish whether the measurements help patients.

uncertain: Can complementary measures adequately distinguish disconnected experience from experience that cannot be reported?
What error rates, detection delays and levels of uncertainty are acceptable for particular clinical decisions?
Would measurements validated during anesthesia also work in people with brain injury or other neurological conditions?

page.title: Real-time monitoring of conscious experience during anesthesia
page.definition: A noninvasive monitor continuously estimates whether a patient under anesthesia perceives the surroundings (connected consciousness), has an internal experience such as a dream without perceiving the surroundings (disconnected consciousness), or would report no experience on awakening. The bispectral index, a current scalp EEG measure, gives a single number correlated with depth of hypnosis. In validation, only an explicit report of no experience establishes the third category. Missing or ambiguous reports leave the state unresolved.

goal.need: After intubation under general anesthesia, 12 of 260 adults moved a hand on command and five signaled pain. None of the 253 questioned after surgery recalled an intraoperative event. Muscle paralysis can conceal awareness, and depth-monitor readings overlap between patients who perceive their surroundings and those who are dreaming. If clinicians could distinguish these experiences reliably in an individual patient, they could reassess the anesthetic while the patient perceives surgery and avoid increasing the dose solely because the patient is dreaming.

completion.title: Independent testing replicates real-time three-state experience monitoring above chance during surgery.
completion.criterion: A noninvasive monitor produces continuous three-state estimates during surgery, before reference elicitation. In prospective surgical-patient testing, connected versus disconnected experience and disconnected versus an explicit report of no experience each have a receiver-operating-characteristic area under the curve (AUC) whose 95% confidence interval lies wholly above 0.5. An independent team reproduces both results in new surgical patients. References use command responses and structured awakening interviews; absent or ambiguous reports remain unclassified.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; no external completion criterion for the full three-state capability was located.
completion.basis: Searches of NAP5, APSF recommendations, FDA BIS indications, registered consciousness studies and standards/prize criteria found no published acceptance test for real-time three-state monitoring. This Atlas minimum extends the laboratory AUC benchmark to prospective surgical use and independent replication. It establishes report-defined discrimination; no clinical accuracy or latency acceptance limit was found.

milestones.title: Scalp EEG distinguishes disconnected experience from no reported experience above chance.
milestones.criterion: During dexmedetomidine sedation, compare 1–4 Hz EEG power at the midline occipital electrode (Oz) over the 20 seconds before each awakening interview. For distinguishing disconnected experience from an explicit report of no experience, the lower bound of the bootstrapped 95% confidence interval for the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUC) must exceed 0.5. Exclude absent or ambiguous reports.
milestones.set_by: UN-CONSCIOUS investigators, published analysis of NCT03284307. The registered primary endpoint was a difference in posterior EEG delta power.

milestones.title: EEG distinguishes both experiential contrasts above chance in pooled propofol and sleep recordings.
milestones.criterion: Train EEG classifiers on dexmedetomidine recordings and test them on held-out propofol and natural-sleep recordings pooled together. For connected versus disconnected experience and for disconnected experience versus an explicit report of no experience, the lower bound of each 95% AUC confidence interval must exceed 0.5. Use waking baseline as the connected reference for the sleep condition. Exclude absent or ambiguous reports.
milestones.set_by: UN-CONSCIOUS investigators, published secondary validation analysis of NCT03284307.
milestones.threshold_quote: we calculated 95% CIs for the AUC of each ROC and compared against chance levels of 0.5.

milestones.title: A monitor distinguishes three report-defined experiential states above chance prospectively during surgery.
milestones.criterion: In one prospective surgical-patient study, record continuous noninvasive three-state estimates before eliciting command responses or conducting structured awakening interviews. For connected versus disconnected experience and for disconnected experience versus an explicit report of no experience, the lower bound of each 95% AUC confidence interval must exceed 0.5. Leave absent or ambiguous reports unclassified.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; no published prospective surgical protocol setting three-state acceptance limits was found.

not_found: No society, regulator, standard or prize criterion was found specifying accuracy and latency limits for the full three-state monitor.
No prospective surgical validation with independent replication of both experiential distinctions was located.

results.finding: In 20 dexmedetomidine-sedated volunteers, Oz delta power distinguished disconnected experience from no experience with an AUC of 0.605.
results.detail: The abstract gives 0.5–4 Hz, while the full primary-outcome methods specify 1–4 Hz at Oz for this analysis.
results.quote:
Occipital delta power showed a weak classification for disconnected and unconscious states (
Fig 3
d), the primary outcome, for Dex (AUC for the ROC 0.605 [95% CI: 0.516; 0.694]).

results.finding: In pooled propofol (n=6) and natural-sleep (n=15) testing, 0.5176 was the smaller of the two 95% AUC lower bounds.
results.quote: These findings generalised to sleep/propofol (validation data set: sensory disconnection [AUC 0.743 {95% CI: 0.6784; 0.8050}]) and unconsciousness (AUC 0.622 [95% CI: 0.5176; 0.7238]).
